q: Despite its reputation, which major Cote de Nuits village has no Grand Cru at all?
exp: It gave the Cote its name and has a string of fine Premiers Crus, but no Grand Cru was granted.

q: Chambolle-Musigny's wines are usually described in which terms?
opts: Massive, tannic and slow to open
exp: Thinner, more limestone-rich soils give a lacier texture, and Chambolle is often called the most ethereal of the Cote de Nuits. Its Grands Crus are Musigny and Bonnes-Mares, the latter shared with Morey-Saint-Denis.

q: Morey-Saint-Denis sits between which two villages?
exp: Squeezed between two famous neighbours, and long overlooked for that reason. It holds four Grands Crus wholly its own, plus the Morey slice of Bonnes-Mares.

q: Which village is dominated by a single walled Grand Cru of about fifty hectares?
exp: Clos de Vougeot is the largest Grand Cru of the Cote de Nuits, walled by the Cistercians, and now divided among some eighty owners.

q: Which appellation is unusual in Burgundy for permitting red, white and rose?
exp: Marsannay at the northern end of the Cote de Nuits is the only one of the Cote d'Or village appellations covering all three colours.
Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Beze are the two senior Grands Crus, with seven others permitted to append the Chambertin name.

q: Which three neighbouring villages are the heartland of great white Burgundy?
exp: The finest Chardonnay in the world is made along a stretch of a few kilometres. Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet take their names from the hill they share. Meursault is the broadest in style, Puligny the most precise.

q: Meursault differs from its two white neighbours in which respect?
opts: It is not in the Cote de Beaune
exp: Its best sites, Perrieres, Genevrieres and Charmes, are Premiers Crus. Many consider Perrieres to merit promotion.

q: Volnay is best known for wines of what character?
exp: Volnay is the Chambolle of the Cote de Beaune. Its neighbour Pommard is the sturdier, firmer counterweight.

q: Pommard's reds are typically described how, relative to Volnay?
exp: More clay in the soil gives a broader, more tannic wine. The pair are the standard illustration of how quickly Burgundy changes across a boundary.

q: Corton is notable as which sort of Grand Cru?
opts: The smallest Grand Cru in Burgundy by area
The Cote de Beaune's only red Grand Cru
exp: The hill of Corton carries the red Corton and the white Corton-Charlemagne, and it is by far the largest Grand Cru area in Burgundy.

q: Which charitable institution holds a famous annual wine auction in Beaune?
opts: The Confrerie des Chevaliers du Tastevin
exp: Founded in 1443 as a hospital for the poor, endowed with vineyards over the centuries. The November auction sets a mood for the vintage.

q: Santenay lies at which end of the Cote de Beaune?
opts: It is not in the Cote de Beaune
exp: The southern extremity, where the Cote d'Or gives way to the Cote Chalonnaise, and traditionally a source of value.

q: Which village name appears attached to both a red-producing and a white-producing reputation, split across the Montrachet hill?
exp: Chassagne was historically a red-wine village and is now better known for white, while retaining a substantial red production.

q: Romanee-Conti and La Tache are the monopoles of which domaine?
exp: A monopole is a vineyard in a single owner's hands, which is rare in fragmented Burgundy and part of what these two names trade on.

q: Montrachet is unusual among Grands Crus in that it does what?
exp: It sits across the boundary of Puligny and Chassagne, which is why both villages appended the name.
